newsitem.title: BELGIUM: HK opposition leader calls for EU unity on China.
newsitem.headline: HK opposition leader calls for EU unity on China.

text.p: Hong Kong Democratic Party leader Martin Lee on Thursday urged European Union nations to "speak with one voice" in opposing China's plans to dilute the British colony's civil liberties after its handover on June 30.
"If Europe speaks together, then individual governments have more confidence to act," Lee told a news conference during a visit to Belgium. "It would be better for Brussels to express concern."

Lee, on a tour of Europe to drum up opposition to China's plans to scrap or amend 25 Hong Kong laws ahead of the territory's return to rule from Beijing, said European governments should act before it was too late.
Beijing's plans have sparked outrage in the British colony and forceful objections from London and its allies, but Lee said the criticism had come too late.

"The British condemnation has come late in the day," he said. "This allowed other governments to delay their reaction but you must realise that China can change -- will change -- if people keep pushing.
In Hong Kong earlier on Thursday, in his strongest worded attack yet, the colonial governor, Chris Patten, lashed at China's "repugnant" proposal to change the territory's bill of rights.

His designated successor and Hong Kong's post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, who is visiting Beijing for a crucial meeting to discuss the laws, argued in defence that the international community had misconstrued the situation.
"Nobody who has spent more than a few minutes in Hong Kong over the last few days can be in any doubt that they (the proposals) are repugnant to the community," Patten said.
Tung said: "I think there are certain sectors of people around the world who are concerned. But I think they are being misled."
Tung was in Beijing for a two-day meeting of the Preparatory Committee, the 150-strong China-appointed caucus responsible for shaping Hong Kong's future in the countdown to the handover.
The question of the laws is high on the agenda.
Lee warned that China's proposals were totally against the autonomy promised Hong Kong in the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration governing the handover.

The treaty embodies Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's "one country, two systems" vision which promises Hong Kong people will run Hong Kong and will be permitted to maintain their freedoms and capitalist way of life intact for 50 years.
Lee said China's real aim was "for control, total control of Hong Kong and that means no freedom of speech, no freedom of assembly, no freedom to demonstrate".
Lee, who has visited the European Parliament in Strasbourg during this trip and will also travel to Germany, Italy, Sweden and Denmark, said he had been well recieved but "hoped for more action".
"It is not for me to tell Europe what to do, but I would like to see more response," he said.
